name: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple
tagline: Kerala’s best‑known serpent shrine set inside a living kavu with a hereditary female priesthood.
summary: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple, Haripad (Alappuzha): a famous serpent shrine in a sacred kavu, known for thousands of naga images, Ayilyam rites and the hereditary Mannarasala Amma.
description: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple stands inside a dense sacred grove (kavu) near Haripad in Alappuzha district. The shrine centres on ancestral serpent worship (Nagaraja and related Nagadevatas) and is notable for the many small serpent images placed along the grove paths and among trees.

The temple remains an active pilgrimage site. Ritual life links the temple compound, the Mannarasala Illam (the ancestral household) and a matriarchal ritual office (the Mannarasala Amma). Devotees commonly attend Ayilyam observances, present serpent votive images, turmeric and urulis, and take part in Noorum Palum and other naga‑vazhipad rites.

history.significance: Mannarasala is one of Kerala’s principal serpent shrines; local tradition connects the temple to the Parashurama account of Kerala’s origin and to the Mannarasala Illam’s hereditary ritual role.

timeline.event: Local tradition states that Parasurama placated the Serpent King (Nagaraja) and that the deity took residence at the grove now called Mannarasala; the Illam family and a matriarchal priestly role grow from this tale.
Mannarasala appears in colonial travel and administrative records (visited by missionary accounts and recorded in Travancore censuses and manuals).
Temple festival records note a Sarpam Pattu (serpent song ritual) observed in 1151 M.E. (1976 C.E.) as a major, widely attended ceremony.
The Mannarasala Illam and temple publish calendars, darshan information and maintain an official website and visitor information; festivals continue on the ayanam/asterism calendar.

keyFacts: The temple’s postal address is Mannarasala P.O., Haripad, Alappuzha, PIN 690514.
The temple is served by the Mannarasala Illam; the temple website names the woman of the Illam (Mannarasala Amma / Valia Amma) as the hereditary ritual head.

folklore.title: The origin of the Mannarasala deity and the Illam
story: By temple tradition, Parasurama reclaimed the land of Kerala and propitiated the Serpent King (Nagaraja). Nagaraja agreed to dwell in a sacred grove at Mannarasala.

Another strand of the local account tells of a household couple, Vasudeva and Sreedevi, who cared for injured snakes and were blessed with a five‑hooded serpent child. That child entered samadhi (permanent meditation) within the Illam’s Nilavara (cellar).

The deity is said to have instructed that the mother of the household should perform his worship; this instruction forms the basis for the hereditary female ritual head (Mannarasala Amma) and the Illam’s special rites.
folklore.note: This account is the temple’s traditional history; versions and emphases differ among local retellings and older sources. See the temple’s history page for the standard temple version.

spiritual.summary: Devotional life at Mannarasala revolves around naga worship: offerings such as Noorum Palum, turmeric, uruli vessels and serpent pratimas; monthly Ayilyam observances; and larger Ayilyam festivals and special rites (Sarpam Pattu). The kavu setting supports quiet walking and respectful observation under temple rules.

experiences.title: Amma darshan and scheduled poojas
experiences.text: Attend Amma darshan at the published times to observe the Valia Amma (hereditary priestly matriarch) performing core rites, receive prasadam and witness Ayilyam day poojas when scheduled.

experiences.title: Observe and present authorised naga offerings
experiences.text: Buy authorised vazhipad items from the temple counters (serpent images, turmeric, urulis) and present them at the designated places; watch Noorum Palum and other serpent‑vazhipad rites led by temple staff or the Illam family.

experiences.title: Walk the kavu and view serpent pratimas
experiences.text: Walk the marked grove paths to see the thousands of small naga images and sacred trees; keep to roped or signposted routes and do not enter protected or private areas of the Illam.

spiritual.bestFor: Pilgrims seeking traditional naga‑vazhipads (fertility, thanksgiving), devotees of naga and Shaiva/Vaishnava traditions, and visitors interested in Kerala ritual, women’s hereditary priesthoods and sacred grove ecology.
mindfulTips: Confirm darshan times and festival dates on the temple’s official website before travel; festival dates follow the lunar/asterism calendar and change each year.
Photography and videography are strictly prohibited within the temple compound except with prior written permission from the temple authorities.
Buy offerings only from authorised temple stalls; external ritual items are not permitted inside the shrine area.
Respect roped or marked areas: certain groves and the Illam’s inner spaces are off‑limits to visitors and reserved for family rites.

highlights: The living kavu (sacred grove) with thousands of small serpent images (naga pratimas) along the paths.
The Mannarasala Amma (Valia Amma), the hereditary female ritual head of the Mannarasala Illam.
The Ayilyam observances (monthly and the larger Kanni/Thulam/Kumbham Ayilyam festivals) culminating in Ezhunnallathu processions and Noorum Palum rites.
Sarpam Pattu — a major serpent song ritual recorded in temple festival history and observed as a rare, significant event.

visitorInfo.bestTime: To see festival rites, plan for Ayilyam days in Kanni (around Sep–Oct), Thulam (Oct–Nov, Thulam Ayilyam is the major festival) and Kumbham (Feb–Mar). Maha Shivaratri (Feb–Mar) is another busy period. Always confirm exact dates and the programme on the temple calendar before travelling.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Mannarasala is a short drive from Haripad town. The nearest railway station is Haripad (HAD), about 2–3 km by road; KSRTC buses serve Haripad town and local taxis/autos connect to the temple. The nearest major airport is Cochin International Airport (approx. 100–120 km by road). For backwater boat travel, use Alappuzha services and combine with a road transfer (Alappuzha is significantly farther inland by road).
etiquette: Wear modest, appropriate clothing in line with Hindu temple customs; avoid shorts and revealing clothes and follow directions from temple staff.
Photography and videography are strictly prohibited within the temple compound except with prior written permission from the temple authorities.
Do not enter roped or marked sacred groves and Illam areas that are closed to the public; follow signs and staff instructions.
Purchase authorised vazhipad items at the temple counters; the temple requests devotees use only authorised ritual items and counters.
visitorInfo.duration: Allow 1–3 hours for darshan, a walk in the kavu and purchasing offerings; on busy Ayilyam festival days allow 2–4 hours or more for queues and ceremonies.

byTrain: Nearest station: Haripad Railway Station (station code: HAD). Station‑to‑temple distance approximately 2–3 km (short drive or auto). Sources: Mannarasala devotee information and railway listings.
byBus: KSRTC Haripad Bus Station (Haripad town) is the local bus hub; the temple is a short taxi/auto ride from the bus stand (approx. 2–3 km). Confirm KSRTC schedules and local connections before travel.
byWater: Mannarasala is inland from the Alappuzha backwaters. If combining houseboat/backwater travel, use Alappuzha boat services (Alappuzha town is approx. 25–35 km by road) and arrange a road transfer from the jetty to Haripad/Mannarasala.
byAir: Cochin International Airport (COK) is the nearest major airport for most travellers; road distance is roughly 100–120 km depending on route. Confirm airport transfer options and travel time in advance.
